claims.text: High-temperature degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is governed primarily by selective chromium oxidation kinetics, with secondary roles for aluminum and titanium.
The selectively oxidized elements control the formation and stability of a protective metastable oxide scale on the fcc matrix.
An oxidizing atmosphere rapidly produces a dense Cr-rich, possibly mixed Cr/Al, oxide scale.
The oxide scale formed in an oxidizing atmosphere mitigates further internal degradation.
Reducing gases suppress stable protective-scale formation.
Under reducing conditions, preferential near-surface chromium depletion through internal diffusion causes microstructural degradation.
The as-built target alloy is a single-phase fcc solid solution.
Fine-scale features in the as-built microstructure underpin the alloy's strength and fatigue resistance.
Exposure at approximately 850–1000 °C is sufficient to activate oxidation and diffusion kinetics in the target alloy.
The proposed 850–1000 °C exposures can be conducted without causing bulk phase transformations in the target alloy.
Oxide-scale formation, thickness, adhesion, and chemistry mediate elemental transfer between the alloy and the gas environment.
A Cr-rich oxide formed under oxidizing conditions is adherent and self-healing and therefore limits further oxidation and internal diffusion.
Reducing conditions promote localized internal oxidation and microstructural weakening despite suppressing the external protective scale.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a continuous, adherent scale with minimal spallation and slower internal degradation.
Reducing exposure will produce thinner or discontinuous scales, near-surface chromium depletion, and more porosity or crack initiation than oxidizing exposure.
The proposed contrast is expected only when oxygen potentials differ enough to alter scale formation substantially.
Temperatures well outside 850–1000 °C or only marginal changes in oxygen potential may not produce the predicted contrast.
